name: CUET UG
approxCandidates: 15.69 lakh registered and 11.64 lakh appeared (CUET UG 2026)
eligibility: Passed or appearing in Class 12 (or equivalent). No age limit. Each university sets its own subject and percentage requirements.

notification.summary: CUET UG 2026 was held in CBT mode from 11 May 2026. Some papers were rescheduled to 31 May and 6–7 Jun because of Eid-ul-Azha. The result was declared on 23 Jun 2026: 15,68,867 candidates registered and 11,64,098 appeared. University admissions and counselling for 2026–27 are complete or wrapping up. The CUET UG 2027 notification is expected around Jan–Feb 2027 (the 2026 notification came out on 3 Jan 2026). Dates come from news reports via web search; cuet.nta.nic.in could not be reached from the research sandbox.
notification.source: https://cuet.nta.nic.in (official). Result figures from the NTA press release as reported by IANS (ianslive.in, 23 Jun 2026) and ETV Bharat.

pattern.notes: Since 2025, every CUET UG test has 50 compulsory questions in 60 minutes, scored +5 / −1. Candidates choose up to 5 tests from 37 (13 languages, 23 domain subjects and the General Aptitude Test). This mock combines two of those tests, the General Test and English, into a 120-minute, 100-question paper, and each section can also be run on its own in 60 minutes. Domain subjects follow the Class 12 NCERT syllabus and are not covered here. The question bank holds 60 original questions (30 per section). Scores are normalised percentiles per test.

trendAnalysis.summary: CUET UG 2024 was held in hybrid mode (pen-and-paper and CBT) with optional questions. From 2025 NTA reverted to CBT only, made all 50 questions compulsory with 60 minutes per test, and cut the maximum number of tests to 5, and 2026 continued this format. The General Test is easy to moderate: quantitative questions stay at about Class 8–10 level (percentages, ratio, averages, SI/CI, speed), and logical reasoning (series, coding, blood relations, directions, seating, syllogisms) has grown to roughly a third of the paper. GK has shifted towards static polity, history, geography and science, plus space and national schemes for current affairs. The English test is dominated by 2–3 reading passages (factual, narrative and literary), with the rest covering vocabulary, error spotting, voice and narration, idioms and sentence rearrangement. Time pressure rather than difficulty is the main challenge.

topics.topic: Grammar: Error Detection, Fill-ups, Voice & Narration

resources.notes: During the answer-key challenge window, NTA publishes the shift-wise question papers with provisional keys and each candidate's recorded responses on cuet.nta.nic.in. Final keys accompany the result. NTA does not keep a permanent public archive, so most full papers in circulation are memory-based or coaching reconstructions. The official syllabus PDFs for all 37 tests are on cuet.nta.nic.in.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India abolishes 'untouchability' and forbids its practice in any form?
questions.explanation: Article 17 abolishes untouchability. Article 14 guarantees equality before law, Article 21 life and personal liberty, and Article 32 constitutional remedies.

questions.question: The Tropic of Cancer does NOT pass through which of the following Indian states?
questions.explanation: The Tropic of Cancer passes through Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram. It does not pass through Bihar.

relevance.note: Tropic of Cancer NOT through Bihar with Jharkhand/Tripura/Mizoram traps; CUET geography format

questions.question: In which year was the Reserve Bank of India established?

questions.question: When the words Bridge, Brick, Bright, Bride and Brief are arranged in dictionary order, which word comes third?

questions.question: 1 January 2025 was a Wednesday. What day of the week was 1 January 2026?
questions.explanation: 2025 is not a leap year, so it has 365 days = 52 weeks + 1 day. The day therefore moves forward by one, to Thursday.

relevance.note: Non-leap year +1 day -> Thursday; CUET calendar item

questions.question: What is 25% of 480 plus 40% of 250?
questions.explanation: 25% of 480 = 120 and 40% of 250 = 100, so the total is 220.

relevance.note: 120+100=220; simple percentage computation

relevance.note: SI 1440; plain formula item

questions.question: The average of five numbers is 18. When one number is removed, the average of the remaining four becomes 16. What is the number that was removed?
questions.explanation: Total of five = 90 and total of four = 64, so the removed number is 90 − 64 = 26.

relevance.note: Removed number 90-64=26; CUET average item

relevance.note: 20 m/s = 72 km/h with unconverted-20 trap; CUET speed item

questions.question: The circumference of a circle is 44 cm. What is its area? (Take π = 22/7.)
questions.explanation: 2πr = 44 gives r = 7 cm, so the area is (22/7) × 49 = 154 cm².

relevance.note: r=7 from circumference, area 154 with diameter traps

questions.question: How many cubes of edge 2 cm can be packed into a closed box with inner dimensions 10 cm × 8 cm × 6 cm?

relevance.note: Packing 5×4×3=60 cubes with 480 volume trap

questions.question: What is the smallest number that must be added to 1000 to make it exactly divisible by 37?
questions.explanation: 37 × 27 = 999, so 1000 leaves a remainder of 1. Adding 37 − 1 = 36 gives 1036 = 37 × 28.

relevance.note: 1000 = 37×27+1, add 36 with remainder trap 1

questions.question: Find the next number in the series: 4, 9, 19, 39, 79, ?
questions.explanation: Each term is (previous × 2) + 1, so 79 × 2 + 1 = 159.

relevance.note: ×2+1 series -> 159; CUET series

questions.question: In a certain code, TEACHER is written as VGCEJGT. How is STUDENT written in that code?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves two places forward (T→V, E→G, …). So S→U, T→V, U→W, D→F, E→G, N→P, T→V, giving UVWFGPV.

relevance.note: +2 letter shift STUDENT -> UVWFGPV with near-miss traps

questions.question: A is B's sister. C is B's mother. D is C's father. E is D's mother. How is A related to D?
questions.explanation: A is a daughter of C (B's mother), and C is D's child. So A is D's granddaughter.

relevance.note: Chain relation -> granddaughter; CUET blood relation

questions.question: Riya walks 10 m north, turns right and walks 6 m, then turns right again and walks 18 m. How far is she now from her starting point?
questions.explanation: She ends 6 m east and 18 − 10 = 8 m south of the start. Distance = √(6² + 8²) = 10 m.

relevance.note: 6-8-10 triple after turns -> 10 m; CUET direction item

questions.question:
Statements: All roses are flowers. Some flowers are red.
Conclusions: I. Some flowers are roses. II. Some roses are red.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
options: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation: 'All roses are flowers' implies that some flowers are roses, so I follows. The red flowers need not include any roses, so II does not follow.

relevance.note: Only I by conversion; CUET syllogism

questions.question: In a row of 40 students, Ravi is 12th from the left end. What is his position from the right end?
questions.explanation: Position from the right = 40 − 12 + 1 = 29.

relevance.note: 40-12+1 = 29th with 28 trap; CUET ranking

questions.question: Five friends P, Q, R, S and T sit in a row facing north. S sits in the middle. Q sits immediately to the right of P. R sits at one of the ends and to the left of S. T is not at either end. Who sits at the extreme right end?
questions.explanation: Since S is 3rd and R is at an end to the left of S, R is 1st. P and Q must be adjacent (P then Q), so they take positions 4 and 5. T fills position 2. The order is R, T, S, P, Q, so Q is at the extreme right.

relevance.note: R-T-S-P-Q -> Q at right end; unique solution, CUET seating

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer.

"Microplastics – fragments smaller than five millimetres – have now been found from the summit of Everest to the floor of the Mariana Trench. Some are manufactured at that size, such as the microbeads once common in face scrubs; most, however, are the result of larger items breaking down under sunlight and waves. Because they are so small, they are easily swallowed by plankton and fish, and they can carry toxic chemicals that cling to their surfaces. Scientists are still debating how seriously they threaten human health, partly because measuring particles this tiny in blood or tissue is technically difficult. What is not in doubt is that their quantity is rising: global plastic production has roughly doubled in two decades, and only a small fraction is recycled. Many researchers therefore argue that the most effective remedy is not better clean-up technology but producing less plastic in the first place."

According to the passage, most microplastics come from:
options: Larger plastic items breaking down under sunlight and waves
Plastic manufactured at a very small size
questions.explanation: The passage says some are manufactured small, but 'most, however, are the result of larger items breaking down under sunlight and waves'.

relevance.note: Detail retrieval with microbead trap; CUET factual passage

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer.

"When Meera's grandfather retired from the railways, he did something no one expected: he bought an old harmonium and enrolled in a music class full of ten-year-olds. The children giggled at first when the white-haired man fumbled with the simplest scales. He laughed along with them. Every evening, while the rest of the family watched television, the slow, wheezing notes of 'Sa Re Ga Ma' drifted from his room. Meera, embarrassed, once asked him why he bothered at his age. 'For forty years,' he said, 'I made sure trains arrived on time. Now I want to arrive somewhere myself.' Two winters later, at the colony's annual function, he played a full raga without a single mistake. Meera, sitting in the front row, was the first to stand up and clap."

What did Meera's grandfather do after retiring?
options: He started teaching music to children
He began organising the colony's annual function
He took a job at the railway station
He bought a harmonium and joined a music class
questions.explanation: The opening sentence says he bought an old harmonium and enrolled in a music class full of ten-year-olds.

relevance.note: Narrative event retrieval with 'teaching music' trap

questions.question: Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F sit around a circular table facing the centre. B sits to the immediate left of A. C sits opposite A. D sits to the immediate right of A. E is not an immediate neighbour of D. Who sits to the immediate right of C?
questions.explanation: Going clockwise (which is each person's left when facing the centre): A, B, _, C, _, D. E cannot sit next to D, so E is between B and C, and F is between C and D. C's immediate right (anticlockwise) is E.

relevance.note: Circular arrangement: E right of C; uniquely determined

questions.question: Choose the number that completes the analogy: 7 : 50 :: 9 : ?

relevance.note: n^2+1 analogy -> 82 with 81 trap

questions.question:
Find the missing number.

Row 1: 3, 5, 13
Row 2: 4, 6, 22
Row 3: 7, 3, ?
questions.explanation: In each row, the third number = first × second − 2: 3 × 5 − 2 = 13, 4 × 6 − 2 = 22, so 7 × 3 − 2 = 19.

relevance.note: Row rule a×b-2 -> 19; CUET missing-number

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer.

"In the early 1990s, India was home to tens of millions of vultures. Within about fifteen years, the populations of three common species had fallen by more than ninety-five per cent. For a long time the cause was a mystery; disease and pesticides were both suspected. The answer, when it came, was surprising: diclofenac, a cheap painkiller given to sick cattle. Vultures feeding on the carcasses of treated animals suffered kidney failure and died within days. The loss was not merely ecological. Vultures had quietly served as a free sanitation service, stripping a carcass to the bone in hours. As they vanished, carcasses rotted in the open, feral dog populations grew on the abundant food, and cases of rabies rose. India banned veterinary diclofenac in 2006 and later restricted other harmful drugs as well, while breeding centres began raising vultures in captivity for release into the wild. Recovery, however, is slow: a vulture pair raises only one chick a year, and the illegal use of human diclofenac on cattle has not entirely stopped. The story is a reminder that the value of a species is often understood only after it is gone."

According to the passage, what was the main cause of the decline of vultures in India?
options: A disease spread by feral dogs
A painkiller given to cattle, which poisoned vultures that ate their carcasses
The loss of trees for nesting
questions.explanation: The passage says the cause was diclofenac, a painkiller given to cattle; vultures that fed on treated carcasses died of kidney failure. Disease and pesticides were only suspected earlier.

relevance.note: Cause (diclofenac) with suspected-cause traps from passage; CUET factual item

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer.

"Arjun had practised his speech for the inter-school debate for two weeks, reciting it to the mirror, to his younger sister and once, to his great embarrassment, to the family's bewildered cat. On the morning of the contest his hands were cold and his mouth was dry. When his name was called, he walked to the podium, looked at the sea of faces and found that the first line of his speech had simply vanished. For three long seconds there was silence. Then, from the third row, he saw Mrs D'Souza, his English teacher, nod slowly, the way she did in class when someone was on the right track. Arjun put away his notes. Instead of the polished opening he had memorised, he told the audience about the morning he had spent rehearsing to a cat. A ripple of laughter ran through the hall, and with it his fear seemed to drain away. The rest of the speech came back to him, not word for word, but in his own voice. He did not win the first prize; that went to a confident girl from another school whose arguments were sharper than his. But as he stepped down, Mrs D'Souza caught his eye and said, 'Today you stopped reciting and started speaking.' Arjun understood that this was a prize of a different kind."

What happened when Arjun first stood at the podium?
options: He dropped his notes on the floor
He forgot the first line of his speech
The audience began to laugh at him
He saw his sister in the audience
questions.explanation: Looking at the audience, he found that the first line of his speech had "simply vanished".

relevance.note: Event at podium with passage-word traps; CUET narrative

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to OBSOLETE.
questions.explanation: Obsolete means no longer in use, i.e. outdated. "Obscure" (unclear or little known) only looks similar.

relevance.note: Obsolete with look-alike 'obscure' trap; exactly the E05 archetype

questions.question: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to AMPLE.
questions.explanation: Ample means more than enough; the opposite is insufficient. The other options are near-synonyms.

relevance.note: Ample antonym with near-synonym distractors; CUET format

questions.question: Choose the correct word to fill the blank: "The new policy is expected to have a positive ______ on exports."
questions.explanation: A noun is needed after "a positive", and the noun meaning "result" is effect. "Affect" is normally a verb.

relevance.note: effect as noun after 'positive'; CUET confused-words item

questions.topic: Grammar: Error Detection, Fill-ups, Voice & Narration
questions.question:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:
"Neither the teacher nor the students / was aware / of the change / in the timetable."
options: Neither the teacher nor the students
questions.explanation: With "neither … nor", the verb agrees with the nearer subject. "Students" is plural, so it should be "were aware".

relevance.note: Neither-nor proximity rule -> 'were'; CUET error-spotting

questions.topic: Grammar: Error Detection, Fill-ups, Voice & Narration
questions.question:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:
"I prefer / tea / than coffee / in the morning."
questions.explanation: "Prefer" takes "to", not "than": I prefer tea to coffee in the morning.

relevance.note: prefer...to not than; named in archetype, CUET classic

questions.topic: Grammar: Error Detection, Fill-ups, Voice & Narration
questions.question: Fill in the blank: "He insisted ______ paying the bill for everyone."
questions.explanation: The verb "insist" is followed by "on" before a gerund: insisted on paying.

relevance.note: insist on; CUET preposition item

questions.topic: Grammar: Error Detection, Fill-ups, Voice & Narration
questions.question: Fill in the blank: "Hardly had I reached the station ______ the train left."
questions.explanation: "Hardly … when" (and "scarcely … when") is the correct pair. "Than" pairs with "no sooner".

relevance.note: Hardly...when with 'than' trap; CUET item

questions.topic: Grammar: Error Detection, Fill-ups, Voice & Narration
questions.question: Choose the correct passive form of: "Who wrote this letter?"
options: By whom was this letter written?
By whom this letter was written?
By whom has this letter been written?
questions.explanation: "Who" becomes "By whom", and the past simple active becomes "was + past participle" with question word order: By whom was this letter written?

relevance.note: Passive of wh-question with word-order trap; CUET voice item

questions.topic: Grammar: Error Detection, Fill-ups, Voice & Narration
questions.question: Choose the correct indirect speech of: She said to me, "Where are you going?"
options: She asked me where was I going.
She said to me where I am going.
She asked me where I am going.
She asked me where I was going.
questions.explanation: "Said to" becomes "asked", the question becomes a statement order (where I was going), and the present continuous shifts to the past continuous.

relevance.note: Reported question word order/backshift with inverted trap

questions.question:
Arrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: fight infections
Q: a balanced diet
R: and stay healthy
S: helps the body
questions.explanation: "A balanced diet (Q) helps the body (S) fight infections (P) and stay healthy (R)."

relevance.note: QSPR fragment ordering; CUET rearrangement

questions.question:
The first sentence is given. Arrange P, Q, R and S to form a coherent paragraph.
1. The town library announced a reading challenge for the summer holidays.
P: By the end of August, more than three hundred children had taken part.
Q: Under its rules, every child who read ten books would receive a certificate.
R: Within a week, the shelves of children's books were almost empty.
S: News of the certificate spread quickly through the neighbourhood schools.
questions.explanation: Q explains the challenge, S (which mentions "the certificate") must follow Q, R describes the immediate rush, and P gives the final result at the end of August.

relevance.note: Certificate must be introduced (Q) before news of it (S): QSRP; CUET paragraph order

questions.question: Choose the one word for: 'a place where bees are kept'.
questions.explanation: An apiary is a place where bees are kept. An aviary houses birds, an aquarium fish, and a granary stores grain.

relevance.note: Apiary vs aviary/aquarium/granary; CUET one-word item

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from the NTA CUET-UG General Test and English papers of 2024, 2025 and 2026 (NTA provisional answer keys with question papers for some shifts, plus shift-wise memory-based analyses by Careers360, PW and Hitbullseye found through WebSearch). Full official papers could not be fetched, so the topic mix and frequencies are estimates combined with the writer's own knowledge of recent CUET papers. From 2025 each test has 50 compulsory questions in 60 minutes. Archetypes describe recurring patterns in our own words; no real question is reproduced. Frequencies are per 50-question test.

archetypes.pattern: Indian Constitution: articles, parts and schedules — which article/part deals with a right or institution
Indian history: year/venue of battles and movements, or arrange events in chronological order
Indian and world geography: rivers (and their nicknames), latitudes passing through states, physical features
Everyday science: composition of air, vitamins and deficiency, units and common phenomena
Art and culture: classical/folk dances, art forms and festivals ↔ state
Current affairs of the previous 12–18 months: summits and hosts, national days, space missions, awards
Economy and institutions: RBI, GST, planning bodies — year of establishment or function
Books and authors / famous personalities
Odd one out from a word/object group (classification by category)
Arrange words in dictionary order and pick the word at a given position
Calendar (day of the week after n years, leap-year trap) or clock-angle problems
Percentage: x% of A ± y% of B, election-vote margins, percentage change
Profit, loss and discount — profit %, successive discounts
Simple and compound interest for 2–3 years
Averages — one value removed/added or replaced
Speed, time and distance — trains, boats and streams, km/h ↔ m/s
Ratio and proportion — combined ratios, partnership shares
Time and work — two people working together
Algebraic identities: value of x² + 1/x², a² + b² from a + b and ab
Mensuration: area/perimeter of circles and triangles, volume of cones/cuboids, packing cubes
Statistics: mean, median, mode of small data sets and their relationship
Number system: divisibility, least number to add/subtract, largest n-digit multiple, remainders
Basic geometry/trigonometry: equilateral-triangle area, standard angles
Number or letter series — next term by ×k + c rule or paired letters
Coding–decoding: letter shift or positional-value coding of words
Blood relations from a chain of statements or a pointing/introducing sentence
Direction sense: walks with turns — final distance and direction (Pythagorean triples)
Two-statement syllogism — which conclusions follow
Ranking and position in a row or class — from top/bottom, left/right
Linear or circular seating arrangement with 5–6 people
Number analogy (n², n³, n² ± 1 relationships)
Missing number in a matrix/figure following an arithmetic rule
Odd number out (squares, primes, multiples)
Factual/discursive passage: detail retrieval and "which is NOT stated"
Factual passage: inference, purpose of a phrase, tone of the author
Vocabulary in context — meaning of a word as used in the passage
Narrative/literary passage: events and characters' actions
Narrative passage: meaning of a quoted line, change in a character's feelings, suitable title
Synonym of a mid-frequency word; distractor that looks or sounds similar
Antonym of a mid-frequency word; distractors include near-synonyms
Choose the correctly spelt word (double letters, -ence/-ance)
Contextual word usage: commonly confused words (affect/effect) in a fill-in
